newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bayer says pre-tax profit to rise 10.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: Bayer says pre-tax profit to rise 10.6 pct.

text.p: Bayer AG chairman Manfred Schneider said the company would meet a target for 1996 pre-tax profit growth of 10.6 percent, bringing it to 4.6 billion marks, French financial daily Les Echos reported.

"In total, we will reach our target of pre-tax profit growth of 10 percent at 4.6 billion marks -- a new historic record for the company," Schneider said in an interview to be published Wednesday morning.

Schneider said that despite his forecast that Bayer's markets would not rebound strongly in the second half of the year, he expected 1996 sales to rise six percent to about 47 billion marks thanks to acquisitions.
Schneider said he did not expect the company to split up or that it would spin off any major units.
"We have decided to remain a diversified but integrated company with well-defined businesses: chemicals, polymers, health and agriculture," he said.
"We are not a conglomerate which needs to be refocused, because in the end we operate in only one sector: chemical/pharmaceutical."
He also said he did not foresee Bayer making a major acquisition but did not rule out a partnership.
"If an opportunity presented itself, I would not hesitate for a second," he said. "But the partnership in question would have to have a portfolio of complementary products."
Schneider said Bayer's Agfa photo affiliate would have to increase its profitability but said no near-term sale of the unit was being considered.

"It is clear that Agfa must improve its profitability. At three percent of turnover, its profitability is insufficient in our view, especially when compared with its competitors Fuji Photo Film Co Ltd or Eastman Kodak Co who are between 12 percent and 13 percent," he said.
"We have given it a target of doubling its profitability in the two to three years ahead. It's only at the end of that time that we will examine possible alternatives."
Schneider said Bayer would apply new sick-pay rules allowed by the government from January 1997.
